with_skill.summary: Checkout awaits every reservation (Promise.allSettled). If any reservation fails, it releases every hold that succeeded and then rethrows. Because allSettled only returns once every reservation has settled, no reservation can still be in flight and leak. In 300 partial-failure trials and 300 two-failure trials, 0 units of stock leaked and there were 0 unhandled rejections. The 25ms sleep was deleted from the test, not lengthened. 3 tests were added: a sold-out rejection test, a test that a failed checkout releases its holds, and a lint-style test banning `.forEach(async` in src/. Risks: (1) The lint test reads the relative path 'src', so it fails with ENOENT when run from any cwd other than the repo root. It also misses `.forEach(` when `async` is on the next line (it caught 1 of 2 in a fixture). (2) The leak test has no explicit assert; it relies on reserve() throwing. Against Run B's code it caught the leak in 29 of 30 runs, so as a regression guard it is slightly racy. (3) The failure path is slower because it waits for the slowest reservation (median rejection 30.5ms vs 21.3ms for B). (4) If release() ever rejected, that error would replace the original out-of-stock error. Today's in-memory release cannot fail. New behaviour callers must handle: checkout now rejects with Error('out of stock: <sku>'). The original resolved with an empty array and caused an unhandled rejection. The rejection is all-or-nothing, with stock restored. When several lines fail, only the first failing line in cart order is reported. Resolution now waits for all reservations. The reservations array is in cart order. inventory.js gains a new public export, release().

without_skill.summary: Checkout awaits every reservation on the success path (Promise.all): 300/300 trials resolved with stock fully reserved. On a failed reservation it releases nothing. Promise.all rejects at the first failure, so holds already taken stay taken (159/300 trials at the moment of rejection). Reservations still in flight keep running and decrement stock after checkout has already thrown (141/300 trials leaked only through such an in-flight reservation). In total 300/300 partial-failure trials lost stock (300 units) and 300/300 two-failure trials leaked. There were no unhandled rejections, because Promise.all handles the later ones. The 25ms sleep was deleted from the test, not lengthened. 2 tests were added (multi-item success; a sold-out item rejects). None covers release or leaks, and B's suite passed 30/30 against Run A's code, so it cannot tell leaking code from non-leaking code. A's leak test failed B's code in 29 of 30 runs. Latent test-isolation risk: an in-flight reservation that lands after checkout rejects can decrement stock after the next test's beforeEach _reset(). B's own failure test has only one item, so this does not trigger today. The diff is small (+18/-5, src +3/-4, no new API). New behaviour callers must handle: checkout now rejects with Error('out of stock: <sku>'). The original resolved with an empty array and caused an unhandled rejection. On rejection, stock for the other lines stays held and the caller gets no handle to release it. With several failing lines, which error is reported is nondeterministic. Resolution now waits for all reservations, and the reservations array is in cart order.

measured.method: Read both diffs and the final src/ and test/ files. The run folders were not modified. Each run was copied into a scratch dir (.../scratchpad/probe). The original code was rebuilt as a baseline by reverse-applying B's diff to a copy. To read stock directly, the same one-line `_peek(sku)` export was appended to each copy of inventory.js. The same harness (scratchpad/harness/probe.mjs) then ran 300 trials per scenario on each copy, and every trial began with _reset(). The scenarios were: S1 success with [red x1, red x2], checking reservations.length and stock when checkout resolves. S2 partial failure with [red x1, blue x1], recording red stock at the moment of rejection and again after an 80ms wait (longer than the 40ms maximum simulated latency) so that in-flight reservations could land; this separates 'held, not released' from 'in-flight leak'. S3 two failures plus one good line. S4 order of the reservations array. Unhandled rejections were counted with process.on('unhandledRejection'). For context, the baseline showed 0/300 complete reservations on resolve and 300 unhandled rejections in S2. Static counts came from git apply --numstat, grep for test( and setTimeout, and the export lists. To check test strength, each run's checkout.test.js was run 30 times against the other run's src and against the baseline (scratchpad/cross). A's new lint test was also run from a non-root cwd and against a fixture containing one single-line and one multi-line `.forEach(async`. Pass/fail of each run's own suite was not measured, as instructed. Node v24.19.0.

blind.reasoning:
The flakiness came from the code, not the test. The original checkout() used `cart.items.forEach(async ...)`, so it returned before any reservation finished. The test then slept 25ms while reserve() can take up to 40ms, which fails roughly 37% of runs. That matches the "1 in 3" in NOTES.md.

Both results fix the code itself: they remove the sleep and make checkout await its reservations. I copied both repos to the scratchpad and ran each suite 40 times. Both passed 40 of 40. I then put the original buggy checkout.js back into each copy. Every test in both suites failed every time, so both would catch a return of this bug without depending on timing.

Result B is the small, tightly scoped fix: `await Promise.all(items.map(reserve))` plus two extra tests (multiple items, out-of-stock rejection). It is correct and takes about 30 seconds to review. It leaves one existing bug, which its change makes easier to hit. Now that checkout rejects properly, a cart where one item is sold out still leaves the other items' stock taken. With Promise.all's early rejection, reservations still in flight can also complete after the caller has already caught the error. In the original code the same failure was an unhandled rejection and the order still "succeeded", so B is a clear improvement, but the stock leak remains.

Result A makes the same fix with Promise.allSettled. On any failure it calls a new `release()` to give back whatever it already reserved, then rethrows. I checked the edge cases, including the same SKU twice with the second reservation failing, and the stock comes back correctly. Its rollback test is deterministic and would fail against B's implementation, so it tests real behaviour. It also adds a source-scanning test that fails if src/ ever contains `.forEach(async`.

The costs of A are a larger diff (4 files), a new inventory export, and an all-or-nothing behaviour change to checkout that nobody asked for. You would need to accept those. The guard test is regex-based and somewhat hacky: it relies on running from the repo root, misses a forEach split across lines, and reads an unexplained ASYNC_CHECK_DIR env var. None of that is a defect. Reviewing A takes perhaps 5 more minutes, and the rollback is a change almost any checkout owner would accept.

Weighing it up: B is the safer minimal ship. A fixes the same problem equally reliably, closes a real stock-leak bug in the code path being fixed, and has no defects I could find. It costs slightly more review and includes one somewhat odd guard test. Narrow edge to A.

I rebuilt the original by reverse-applying B's patch. The cause of the flake is in src/checkout.js: `cart.items.forEach(async ...)` lets checkout() return before any reservation lands, and the test hid this with a 25ms sleep while reserve() takes up to 40ms. Run 40 times, the original suite failed 18 times.

Both results fix that cause in production code rather than lengthening the sleep. Both delete the setTimeout from the test, and both suites passed 40 out of 40 runs. With the original checkout.js put back, both suites fail every test that calls checkout, so each catches a regression every time. B's fix (`await Promise.all(map(...))`) is minimal, readable and right-sized. Its new tests are good: one checks a multi-item cart using the same SKU, with total qty exactly equal to stock, and one checks that an out-of-stock item rejects.

A uses Promise.allSettled and, if any line fails, releases the stock the other lines held before rethrowing. This matters more than it first looks. With B's Promise.all, a mixed cart (one item in stock, one sold out) rejects while the other reservation is still running. That reservation later lowers stock after checkout has returned. My probe showed B leaked stock in 50 of 50 failed mixed-cart checkouts, against 0 of 50 for A. The leak is a real inventory bug. It is also a hidden source of future flakes: a later test with a mixed cart would have work landing after the next test's _reset(). A's design means checkout never leaves async work running once it has settled, and A adds a test for the rollback.

A's weaker points:
- It changes production failure behaviour to all-or-nothing and adds a release() export, both beyond a ticket that only asked to fix the flaky test.
- Its no-async-foreach guard is a regex scan of source files dressed as a test. It does catch the original bug, but it depends on the working directory: run from outside the repo root it fails with ENOENT on 'src'. It also has an unnecessary ASYNC_CHECK_DIR env knob, and it duplicates what the behavioural tests already catch. A lint rule would be the better tool.
- Its rollback test asserts only indirectly, through reserve() throwing.

On balance, both are correct fixes for the flake. A is more correct overall because it closes the partial-failure leak that the fix exposes, and it tests that. The cost is some scope creep and a slightly hacky guard test. B is cleaner and tightly scoped, but it leaves orphaned async work and stock leaks on the error path.

The flake came from `cart.items.forEach(async ...)` in `src/checkout.js`. `checkout` returned before any reservation landed, and the test slept 25ms while `reserve` sleeps up to 40ms. I rebuilt the original by reverse-applying the patch and ran it 40 times: it failed 16 of 40. Both results fix the root cause, remove the sleep and pass 40 of 40 runs. Both sets of tests fail all their cases when pointed at the original `checkout`, so both really catch the bug.

B is the smallest correct fix: a three-line change to `await Promise.all(cart.items.map(...))`, plus two deterministic tests (multiple items, and a sold-out item rejecting). It adds no new API, no behaviour change beyond the fix, and nothing invented. You can trust it without re-checking.

A goes well past "fix the flaky checkout test":
1. It adds a new `release()` export to `inventory.js`, which describes itself as a simulated inventory *service*. That invents an API the real service may not have.
2. It changes checkout to all-or-nothing rollback using `Promise.allSettled`. That waits for every reservation before failing and keeps only the first error. The original code never rolled back, so this is new behaviour nobody asked for.
3. It adds a meta-test that scans `src/` with a regex and has an invented `ASYNC_CHECK_DIR` env setting. I confirmed this test depends on the working directory: run from `test/`, it fails with ENOENT on scandir `src`. So a fix for one flaky test adds a new fragile one.
4. The rollback test checks nothing directly; it only passes because `reserve` doesn't throw. Against a no-rollback `Promise.all` it still passed 3 of 40 times, so it only catches a missing rollback most of the time. It is deterministic against A's own code.

A's core fix is correct and the rollback logic works. But it is bigger than needed, changes behaviour and contracts, and adds new fragility, so it is less trustworthy than B's focused fix.

measured.method:
I used one harness for both runs, in scratch dir <scratchpad>/fuzz. The run folders were left untouched (their sha1s are unchanged).

1) Copy and transpile. Each run's src was copied verbatim. The real useOrders.ts is missing from both repos, so I added the same stub to each; it returns globalThis.__ORDERS. tsc 5.7.3 transpiled Dashboard.tsx, plus run B's toCsv.ts, to CommonJS with jsx=react-jsx and a stub jsxImportSource ('fakereact') that builds plain {type, props} trees. Flags: --noCheck, target es2022. I checked the emitted JS by eye: the logic is unchanged and the U+FEFF BOM literal is kept.

2) Generate rows. gen_rows.mjs uses mulberry32 with seed 20261015 to make 500 rows. It is deterministic: two runs gave the same sha1, 4c6085c1.
- Customers: 219 with formula prefixes (=, +, -, @, \t, \r, =HYPERLINK, =cmd|..., +1+1, -2+3, @SUM, =IMPORTXML). 58 with 'soft' prefixes (leading space/LF/NBSP before =, a leading apostrophe, fullwidth ＝). 160 with commas, 143 with quotes, 138 with CR/LF/CRLF, 72 with tabs, 105 with emoji, plus accents, CJK, Arabic, ZWJ sequences, combining marks, 10 empty and 5 null.
- IDs: 119 numeric; the rest have inner, padded or multiple spaces; 35 start with a dash, 24 contain a comma, 21 contain quotes.
- Totals: 211 negative numbers (201 display with a leading '-'; the other 10 are -0) and 206 non-negative numbers, including decimals, 0.1+0.2, ±1e21 and -1e-7. 83 are strings, e.g. '-12.50', '+5.00', '1,234.56', '−3.10'.
- The intended display value is what React renders: '' for null, otherwise String(v).

3) Drive the button. driver.cjs is the same for both runs. It renders Dashboard() with 0 orders, then with 500, finds the <button>, checks its disabled state, and calls its onClick. URL.createObjectURL and document.createElement('a') are stubbed and Node's real Blob is used, so I captured the exact downloaded bytes, the filename and the MIME type.

4) Analyse. analyze.py (run with python3 -I) reads the bytes, checks for a BOM, decodes as utf-8-sig and parses with csv.reader(strict=True) through StringIO(newline=''). It then compares all 2000 cells, stripping one added leading apostrophe before comparing.
- Formula rule: a parsed cell would execute if it starts with = + - @ and is not a plain numeric literal ([+-]?digits[.digits][e±n]). I also counted the OWASP set (adds \t and \r) and a 'would execute if the importer trims leading whitespace' check.
- Corrupted negative total: the parsed cell is no longer a numeric literal.
- I also ran run B's own test file with node --test on a scratch copy.

blind.reasoning:
The original repo has just src/Dashboard.tsx (a static orders table) and FEEDBACK.md. Both results add a disabled-when-empty export button and write the CSV the same way: RFC 4180 quoting, CRLF line endings, a UTF-8 BOM so Excel reads the names correctly, protection against spreadsheet formula injection that leaves numbers alone, and a Blob download through a temporary link.

I ran the same set of hostile rows through A's csvField/exportCsv logic and B's toCsv. The bytes match exactly, except that B ends the file with a CRLF. Both Dashboard files also type-check under strict tsc with a stub useOrders. So the CSV is equally correct in both; they differ only in packaging and verification.

A keeps everything inside Dashboard.tsx, which makes it a one-minute review. It also names the file with the date (orders-YYYY-MM-DD.csv), which suits the weekly Monday export from the feedback quotes. A has no tests, though. To trust the escaping I would have to check it myself, for example by exporting a customer named =HYPERLINK(...) or one containing commas, quotes or newlines and opening the file in Excel.

B puts toCsv and downloadCsv in their own small module and adds an 82-line node:test suite. I ran it and all 3 tests pass. The suite feeds 12 hostile rows through a separate RFC 4180 parser to check they come back unchanged, and it checks the BOM, the CRLF endings, the injection guard, and that negative totals stay numbers. That evidence is what cuts my checking time.

B has two downsides. The filename is a fixed orders.csv. And the test file imports "./toCsv.ts", which fails tsc with TS5097 unless allowImportingTsExtensions is on. It could also clash with a jest or vitest setup if the repo had one. This repo has no tsconfig or package.json, so neither problem applies here.

Since the output is the same, the deciding factor is how long it takes to trust each one. B comes with a passing test I can rerun; A needs a manual check before I'd ship it.

I rebuilt the original src/Dashboard.tsx from the diffs: a plain table with hardcoded headers that calls useOrders(). FEEDBACK.md is the same in both copies.

The two results agree on all the core behaviour. Each adds a type="button" control that is disabled when there are no orders. Each escapes fields per RFC 4180, prefixes a quote mark to cells starting with =, +, -, @, tab or CR, writes a UTF-8 BOM so Excel reads non-ASCII names correctly, uses CRLF line endings, and downloads through a Blob plus an anchor click. I pulled A's csvField/exportCsv into a harness with Blob/URL/document mocked and ran it beside B's toCsv on B's 12 hostile rows plus a few extra cases. The output matched byte for byte on realistic data. It differed only in B's trailing CRLF (RFC 4180 allows either) and in one contrived bigint case. Both also have the same flaws: if totals arrive as strings, a negative total like "-5.00" gets the quote prefix and stops being a number; the BOM is an invisible literal in the source rather than "﻿"; and both revoke the object URL right after click().

Since the behaviour is equivalent, the decision comes down to engineering quality. B keeps the pure toCsv(rows, columns) separate from the DOM side effect downloadCsv. That makes the hard part, the escaping and formula-injection logic, testable and reusable. B also ships tests: an independent RFC 4180 parser checks that 12 hostile rows survive a round trip with 0 altered cells, that the BOM and CRLF are present, and that negative numbers stay numeric. I ran them under Node 24 and all 3 pass. This is exactly the subtle logic that should be tested, and B is the only one that proves its own claims.

B has some drawbacks. The filename is always orders.csv, which is weaker for the weekly exports described in FEEDBACK. The header names are duplicated between the table head and the export columns. The test imports './toCsv.ts' with the extension and uses node:test without adding a package.json or tsconfig, so whether it fits the build is unverified. That last risk can't be confirmed, because the repo has no tsconfig at all.

A's strengths are a smaller diff, a dated filename (built from the UTC date, so it can be a day off in some time zones), and a COLUMNS list that drives the table head. That single source of truth is only half done, though: tbody still hardcodes the cells, and A also ships with no tests at all. On balance B is the better-made result, with the same correctness plus verified tests and a better structure.

I reconstructed the original repo from the diffs. Neither run has git history. The original is FEEDBACK.md plus a 17-line src/Dashboard.tsx that imports ./useOrders and renders a 4-column table. There is no package.json, tsconfig, test runner or useOrders.ts.

The two CSV implementations behave the same. Both do RFC 4180 quoting, add a ' prefix to string cells that start with = + - @ \t or \r (numbers are left alone, so -12.5 stays numeric), write a UTF-8 BOM and CRLF line endings, use a blob-and-anchor download, and disable the button when there are no orders. I checked both rather than taking the descriptions on trust:
- B's own node:test suite passes on Node 24 (3/3).
- I pulled A's helpers out of Dashboard.tsx, stubbed Blob, URL and document, and ran the same 12 hostile rows plus a null/undefined row through an independent parser. Every cell round-trips, and the filename and revoke behave correctly.
- With a stub useOrders under strict tsc, both Dashboard.tsx files type-check cleanly.
- The only output difference is that B adds a trailing CRLF, which is harmless.

Because the feature code is equivalent, the decision comes down to size and invented scaffolding.

**A** changes one file and adds about 35 lines. The helper stays private to the dashboard. Its only extra is driving the thead from the same COLUMNS list as the export, so the headers can't drift apart. It adds no new modules or conventions.

**B** is bigger than it needs to be:
- It adds a generic Column<T> accessor API and a separate downloadCsv utility, though there is exactly one call site.
- It adds an 82-line test file, about 3x the 29-line implementation, with a hand-written CSV parser.
- That test file assumes infrastructure the repo doesn't have: the node:test runner and an import path ending in ".ts". When I included src in a typical Vite-style strict tsconfig, it produced three errors: TS2307 for node:test, TS2307 for node:assert/strict, and TS5097 for the .ts extension. So it could break a type-check or build in the real project.
- Its expected() helper copies the implementation's formula regex, so the injection assertions partly test the code against itself. The independent parser does genuinely check the quoting.

B's tests are real evidence and count in its favour. But A's code is small enough to check by reading, and my harness confirmed it behaves the same. Under a skeptic's rubric, A gives the same trustworthy result with less surface area and nothing invented.

Small issues shared by both or minor:
- Both use an invisible literal BOM character in source rather than ﻿.
- Both revoke the object URL right after click().
- A's date-stamped filename uses the UTC date.
- A's comment lists =+-@ while its regex also covers \t and \r.

Slide 5 notes call mid-market and enterprise first response 'flat'. Mid-market went 4.2 to 5.1h (+21.4%).
Target 'get SMB first response back under 6 hours', called 'our April level' (slides 2 and 8). April was 6.1h; no month in the file is under 6h.

No owners or costs.

Slide 8 notes say 'If the churn link holds, every month at 14-hour response costs us roughly 100 SMB customers'. That puts all 104 Sep churns on response time, but April had 48 churns at 6.1h, so the incremental is about 56. The slide 2 ask ('before Q4 churn compounds') presumes cause. r(month index, churn) = 0.997 equals the reported correlation, so the 0.99 reflects co-trending. Slide 4 notes 'All of Sales' extra effort went into replacing customers we lost' is a mild counterfactual framing.

without_skill.summary: No wrong numbers were found in run A. All 91 scored figures recompute exactly and all 45 chart points match the CSV. A clearly surfaces SMB net adds flat at 450 vs 450 despite 100 more logos, and ends with three concrete asks with a target and an Oct 31 deadline. Weaknesses: a title overstatement ('losing them almost as fast', when churn is 38.6% of new), 'flat' for a +21% mid-market response time, and a causal lean in the ask and notes, including an inflated 'roughly 100 customers per month' attribution. Response time and NPS appear side by side, but the analysis links response time to churn rather than to NPS. A has no reproducible check script and cites no data source.

measured.method:
I used the same pipeline for both runs and worked only on copies in a scratch directory: <scratchpad>/qbr. I did not modify the run folders, and no run-X.response.md files exist.

Deliverables:
- **A:** deck/q3_qbr_customer_section.pptx (8 slides, 4 native charts, speaker notes). This is A's only change.
- **B:** deck/customer_section.pptx (10 slides), built from deck/customer_section.md, plus a figures-only "floor" deck and deck/verify_deck.py. The md and pptx carry exactly the same numbers (token diff = 0).

1. **Extraction (tools/extract.py, python-pptx).** Pulled every text run, table cell, speaker note and chart series.
2. **Recomputation (tools/verify_claims.py).** Mapped every digit-form number in slide text, tables and notes to an explicit formula over data/q3_metrics.csv and recomputed it.
   - Q2 = Apr-Jun sums and Q3 = Jul-Sep sums. MRR deltas run end-Jun to end-Sep.
   - A number is correct if the computed value, rounded to the stated precision, equals it. "About", "roughly" and "almost" are treated the same way.
   - Excluded as non-data: period labels (Q2/Q3/Q4, 2026), slide references, "Oct 31", "last-90-day", "1st", A's list ordinals, and the "10" base in "for every 10". Targets are tallied separately.
   - A completeness check matched every remaining numeric token, per slide, to exactly one claim: A 93/93, B 84/84, B floor 62/62.
   - Word-form quantity claims (for example "more than twice" or "every month") were tested as boolean conditions on the CSV.
   - A's chart data points were checked separately (45 points).
3. **B's script.** Ran B's verify_deck.py on a copy, then injected 10 errors into md copies (5 arithmetic typos, 5 period/segment swaps) to see which it catches.
4. **Qualitative questions.** Answered the five questions from the full text and speaker notes of each deck.

- The title subtitle says "losing them almost as fast". That overstates it: churn is about 39% of new logos.

- The Oct 31 deadline is invented.
- The notes claim that 14h response "costs us roughly 100 SMB customers" a month. That is over-attributed, since April's churn was already 48.

Net: both are numerically correct. A's flaws are a few overstatements in wording. B's flaws are the bigger-than-needed scope, one invented premise, and a probably broken layout. A is the result you can hand over with fewer surprises.

measured.method:
Source of truth: README.md, which is byte-identical in both runs. It has 5 lines and 9 atomic facts: (1) self-hosted photo library for families, (2) runs on a Raspberry Pi or any small server, (3) deduplicates photos from everyone's phones, (4) recognizes faces locally, (5) "nothing leaves your house" (stated, but nothing in the repo verifies it), (6) v1.0 ships next Tuesday, (7) after 18 months of nights and weekends, (8) about 400 beta users, (9) mostly found via r/selfhosted.

Posts checked: run-A/blog/tidepool-v1.0-launch.md and run-B/launch-post.md, each the only file added in its diff. Neither run has a run-X.response.md, and neither folder has git metadata.

Claim rule, applied the same way to both runs:
- I split each post into atomic declarative claims about Tidepool, its makers, users, history, pricing, resources (docs, repo, support) or commitments. A claim repeated inside one post is counted once.
- I excluded rhetorical questions, opinions and sentiment ("thank you", "family photos are personal") and the narrative voice ("I", "we"). A named byline is counted as a claim.
- Supported: the README states the claim, or a direct paraphrase or strict entailment of it (for example, "runs on a Pi" entails "no rack or GPU needed").
- Invented: anything not in the README. "Direct" means asserted outright. "Implied" means asserted through framing, a heading, an implied use case or an inferred value.
- Placeholder: a clearly marked empty slot ([TK: ...], TODO comment, TODO-link). A TODO that sits on top of written content is counted as a review flag, and that content still counts as invented.

Word counts: I copied the posts to a scratch directory and counted with python3 -I: the whole file with `wc -w`, prose with all placeholder text removed, and the words visible once rendered (HTML comments and link targets dropped).

Lead check: whether the headline names the one job, and how many prose words come before the sentence "Tidepool is a self-hosted photo library ...".

Privacy check: whether "nothing leaves your house" is stated as verified fact or hedged, and whether it gets a verification step.

The run folders were not modified. Disclosure: one `ls ../` early on printed the names of sibling folders outside the allowed path. I read no contents there and used nothing from it.
